title: Salesforce Developer
description: From the data model to PD II: SOQL, Flow, Apex, testing, security, LWC, integration, async and deployment, practised on real problems graded in your org.

nodes.title: How the platform works
nodes.summary: Orgs, metadata versus data, and where developers work.
nodes.lesson:
Salesforce is a **multi-tenant** platform: thousands of companies share the same servers, each in its own **org**. That's why the platform enforces **governor limits**: no one org's code may starve the others.

Two kinds of things live in an org:

- **Metadata**: the shape of the org. Objects, fields, page layouts, Flows, Apex classes. It's moved between orgs by deploying.
- **Data**: the records: the actual Accounts, Contacts and Opportunities.

You'll work in several kinds of org: a free **Developer Edition** for learning, **sandboxes** (copies of production for building and testing), **scratch orgs** (short-lived orgs created from source), and **production**, where real users work. Code is written in a sandbox or scratch org and deployed to production, never written there directly.
concepts: Multi-tenancy, and why it leads to governor limits
Metadata (configuration and code) versus data (records)
Developer Edition, sandbox, scratch org and production: what each is for
pitfalls: Building or testing directly in production: Apex can't even be written there, and Flow changes affect real users at once.
Expecting a sandbox to stay in sync with production: it's a copy from the moment it was refreshed.

quiz.q: Which of these is metadata rather than data?
options: A closed Case with its comments
quiz.why: Fields, objects, layouts, Flows and code describe the org's shape: that's metadata. Records are data.

quiz.q: Why does Salesforce enforce governor limits?
options: Orgs share servers, so no one org may use more than its share
Only for security, so no one can read too much data
quiz.why: Multi-tenancy: limits keep one org's code from slowing everyone else.

quiz.q: Where should new Apex be written and tested?
options: In the Developer Console in production, then copied to a sandbox
In a sandbox or scratch org, then deployed
quiz.why: Production can't even compile new Apex directly; it's built elsewhere and deployed with tests.

nodes.title: Developer tools
nodes.summary: VS Code, the Salesforce CLI and source-driven development.
nodes.lesson:
Modern Salesforce development happens in **VS Code** with the **Salesforce Extension Pack** and the **Salesforce CLI** (`sf`).

- `sf org login web` connects an org; `sf project retrieve start` pulls metadata into files; `sf project deploy start` pushes them back.
- Your project is **source format**: one file per class, trigger, object field, Flow. It belongs in **Git**.
- **Scratch orgs** are created from a definition file, used for a feature, then thrown away. They make every change reproducible.

The Developer Console still works for a quick look at a debug log or a test run, but it isn't where projects live.
concepts: Retrieving and deploying metadata with `sf project retrieve/deploy start`
Source format and why it belongs in Git
Scratch orgs as disposable, reproducible environments
pitfalls: Editing the same class in the org and locally: the next retrieve overwrites one of the versions.
Committing an org's credentials or auth URL to Git.

quiz.q: Which command sends your local metadata to an org?
quiz.why: deploy sends local source to the org; retrieve brings the org's metadata down to files.

quiz.q: What is a scratch org best for?
options: A short-lived, reproducible org for one feature
Replacing sandboxes for UAT with a full copy of real data
quiz.why: Scratch orgs are created from a definition file and source, used briefly, then deleted.

quiz.q: Where should your Salesforce project's source live?
options: In the Developer Console of the production org
quiz.why: Source format in Git gives history, review and reproducible deploys.

nodes.title: Data model
nodes.summary: Objects, fields, relationships and how records connect.
nodes.lesson:
Everything in Salesforce is a **record** of an **object** (Account, Contact, Opportunity, or your own `Thing__c`). Objects have **fields**; custom ones end in `__c`.

Relationships link objects:

- **Lookup**: a loose link (a Contact *looks up* to an Account). Deleting the parent doesn't delete the child.
- **Master-detail**: a tight link. The child inherits sharing and is deleted with the parent; the parent can have **roll-up summary** fields.

You'll query these relationships in SOQL next: child-to-parent with dots (`Account.Name`), parent-to-child with subqueries (`(SELECT Id FROM Contacts)`).
concepts: Standard versus custom objects and fields (`__c`)
Lookup versus master-detail: deletion, sharing and roll-up summaries
Junction objects for many-to-many relationships
Relationship names: `Account.Name` up, `Contacts` down
pitfalls: Choosing master-detail when the child must exist without a parent: master-detail children can't.
Querying a child relationship by the object name (`Contact`) instead of the relationship name (`Contacts`, or `Things__r` for custom).
nodes.diagramCaption: Lookup (Contact to Account), master-detail (Expense to Project) and a junction object (Enrollment) linking Students and Courses many-to-many.

quiz.q: In the diagram, what happens to Expense__c records when their Project__c is deleted?
quiz.why: Master-detail children can't exist without their master, so they're deleted with it.
quiz.imageAlt: Relationships diagram: Expense__c is the detail side of a master-detail relationship to Project__c.

quiz.q: Using the diagram: how do Students relate to Courses?
options: Through Enrollment__c, a junction object with two master-details
A lookup from Student__c to Course__c, one per student
quiz.why: Many-to-many goes through a junction object with a master-detail to each side.
quiz.imageAlt: Relationships diagram: Enrollment__c sits between Student and Course with a link to each.

quiz.q: Which relationship lets a parent have roll-up summary fields?
quiz.why: Roll-up summaries need master-detail (a few standard lookups, like Account to Opportunity, are special cases).

quiz.q: Contact has a lookup to Account. Which SOQL gets each contact's account name?
options: SELECT LastName, (SELECT Name FROM Account) FROM Contact
SELECT LastName FROM Contact JOIN Account
quiz.why: Child to parent uses dot notation through the relationship name.

nodes.title: SOQL basics
nodes.summary: SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY and LIMIT; parent fields with dots.
nodes.lesson:
**SOQL** reads records. Every query names one object and the fields you want:

```sql
SELECT Id, Name, Industry FROM Account WHERE Industry = 'Technology' ORDER BY Name LIMIT 10
```

- `WHERE` filters with `=`, `!=`, `<`, `LIKE 'Ac%'`, `IN ('a','b')`, combined with `AND`, `OR`, `NOT`.
- Parent fields use **dots**: `SELECT LastName, Account.Name FROM Contact`.
- `ORDER BY` sorts; add `NULLS LAST` to push blanks down; `LIMIT` caps rows.
- There's no `SELECT *`: name every field you need. Asking for a field you didn't select raises an error in Apex.
concepts: The shape of a query: SELECT fields FROM object WHERE … ORDER BY … LIMIT …
Comparison operators, LIKE, IN, and combining with AND/OR
Child-to-parent fields with dot notation
Sorting with NULLS FIRST/LAST
pitfalls: Using double quotes for strings: SOQL needs single quotes.
Reading a field in Apex that the query didn't select: `SObjectException`.
Expecting `ORDER BY ... DESC` to put blanks last: it puts them first unless you add `NULLS LAST`.

nodes.title: Security model
nodes.summary: Profiles, permission sets, sharing: what users can do and see.
nodes.lesson:
Salesforce asks two questions before showing a record:

1. **Can this user work with this object and field at all?** That's **object and field permissions**, from the user's **profile** and **permission sets**. Field-level security (FLS) can hide a field everywhere, including the API.
2. **Can they see this particular record?** That's **sharing**: organization-wide defaults set the baseline, then the role hierarchy, sharing rules, manual shares and Apex sharing open access up.

As a developer this matters because **Apex runs in system mode** by default: it ignores object permissions and FLS unless you ask it not to, and `with sharing` decides whether record sharing applies. You'll write secure Apex in the Advanced stage; here, learn the model it protects.
concepts: Object permissions and field-level security, from profiles and permission sets
Organization-wide defaults as the most restrictive baseline
Role hierarchy, sharing rules and manual sharing only open access up
Apex runs in system mode unless told otherwise
pitfalls: Hiding a field only on the page layout: it's still visible in reports, list views and the API. Use field-level security.
Trying to restrict access with a sharing rule: sharing only ever grants more.
nodes.diagramCaption: Record access in layers: organization-wide defaults, then role hierarchy, sharing rules, manual sharing and teams, and Apex managed sharing, each only adding access.

quiz.q: Look at the diagram. Organization-wide default is Private. Can a sharing rule make a record invisible to someone the role hierarchy already lets see it?
options: No: every layer after the defaults only adds access
Yes, a rule can set the record to Private for some users
quiz.why: Sharing is additive: the layers above the defaults grant access; none of them take it away.
quiz.imageAlt: Diagram of access layers: organization-wide defaults first, then four layers that each add access.

quiz.q: Using the diagram, which layer sets the most restrictive baseline?
quiz.why: Organization-wide defaults are layer 1, the baseline everything else builds on.
quiz.imageAlt: Diagram of access layers with organization-wide defaults at the top as layer 1.

quiz.q: A Salary field must be hidden from support users in reports and the API too. What do you use?
options: Remove it from the page layout
quiz.why: Field-level security applies everywhere; layouts only affect that page.

quiz.q: By default, which mode does Apex run in?
options: System mode: it ignores object and field permissions
User mode: it respects the user's permissions
quiz.why: Apex runs in system mode unless you use user-mode queries or other enforcement.

nodes.title: Flow basics
nodes.summary: Record-triggered flows: before-save field updates.
nodes.lesson:
**Flow** is Salesforce's declarative automation, and the first tool to reach for before code.

A **record-triggered flow** runs when a record is created, updated or deleted:

- **Fast Field Updates (before-save)** change fields on the triggering record before it's saved: no extra DML, very fast.
- **Actions and Related Records (after-save)** create or update other records, send emails, call actions.

Entry conditions decide which records start the flow. "**Only when a record is updated to meet the condition requirements**" fires once, when the condition becomes true, instead of on every save.
concepts: Before-save versus after-save record-triggered flows
Entry conditions and when to run the flow
$Record and $Record__Prior
When to prefer Flow over Apex
pitfalls: Using an after-save flow to update the triggering record: it costs an extra save and can re-trigger automation.
Choosing 'every time the condition is met' when you meant 'only when updated to meet': the action repeats on every edit.

nodes.title: Apex basics
nodes.summary: Variables, types, classes, methods and control flow.
nodes.lesson:
**Apex** is Salesforce's strongly typed, Java-like language. It runs on the platform, next to your data.

- Primitive types: `Integer`, `Decimal` (use it for money), `String`, `Boolean`, `Date`, `Datetime`, `Id`.
- Every record type is an **sObject** type: `Account a = new Account(Name = 'Acme');`.
- **Classes** hold methods; `static` methods are called on the class (`MyUtils.format(x)`), instance methods on an object.
- Control flow: `if/else`, `for` (including `for (Account a : accounts)`), `while`, `switch on`.
- SOQL is part of the language: `List<Account> accs = [SELECT Id FROM Account];`, and Apex variables are **bound** with a colon: `WHERE Name = :name`.
- `null` is not zero: calling a method on null throws `NullPointerException`.
concepts: Primitive types, sObjects and when to use Decimal
Static versus instance methods
Inline SOQL and bind variables (`:name`)
Null safety: checking before calling methods
pitfalls: Using `Double` for money: rounding errors. Use `Decimal` with `setScale`.
`String ==` comparison is case-insensitive in Apex; use `.equals()` when case matters.
Calling a method on a value that might be null.

nodes.title: Advanced SOQL
nodes.summary: Aggregates, subqueries, semi-joins and date literals.
nodes.lesson:
- **Aggregates**: `COUNT()`, `SUM()`, `AVG()`, `MIN()`, `MAX()` with `GROUP BY`, filtered after grouping with `HAVING`. In Apex they return `AggregateResult`; read values by alias: `(Decimal) ar.get('total')`.
- **Parent-to-child subqueries**: `SELECT Name, (SELECT LastName FROM Contacts) FROM Account`.
- **Semi-joins and anti-joins**: `WHERE Id IN (SELECT AccountId FROM Opportunity)` and `NOT IN`, to filter by whether related records exist.
- **Date literals**: `TODAY`, `LAST_N_DAYS:30`, `THIS_QUARTER`, evaluated when the query runs.
- **Polymorphic** fields (`WhoId`, `WhatId`) can point to several objects; `TYPEOF` selects fields per type.
concepts: GROUP BY with HAVING, and reading AggregateResult
Child subqueries using the plural relationship name
Semi-joins and anti-joins
Relative date literals
pitfalls: Putting an aggregate in WHERE: use HAVING.
Expecting a child subquery's filter to drop parents with no matching children: it doesn't; use a semi-join.
Hard-coding date ranges that drift; prefer date literals.

nodes.title: Advanced Flow
nodes.summary: Decisions, loops, autolaunched flows, and calling Flow from Apex.
nodes.lesson:
- A **Decision** element takes the first outcome whose conditions match, so order outcomes from most to least specific; the default outcome catches the rest.
- **Loops** walk a collection one item at a time; inside, use Assignment to collect results, then do **one** Create/Update after the loop, not one per item.
- **Autolaunched flows** have no trigger: Apex, other flows or REST call them with input variables and read output variables.
- From Apex: `Flow.Interview f = Flow.Interview.createInterview('My_Flow', inputs); f.start(); f.getVariableValue('result');`.
- Flows share governor limits with the transaction that runs them.
concepts: Decision outcome order and the default outcome
Loops with collections, and DML outside the loop
Input and output variables on autolaunched flows
Calling a flow from Apex
pitfalls: A Create or Update element inside a loop: one DML per item, quickly over the limit.
Forgetting to mark variables available for input or output: callers can't see them.

nodes.title: SOSL search
nodes.summary: Text search across many objects at once.
nodes.lesson:
**SOSL** searches text across several objects in one call, the way the global search box does:

```apex
List<List<SObject>> found = [FIND 'Acme*' IN NAME FIELDS RETURNING Account(Name), Contact(FirstName, LastName)];
```

- Use **SOQL** when you know the object and want exact filters; use **SOSL** when you're searching words across objects or in long text.
- Results come back as a list per object, in the order of `RETURNING`.
- SOSL uses the search index, so very recent records may not appear for a moment.
concepts: When SOSL beats SOQL
FIND, IN … FIELDS and RETURNING
Results as a list of lists
pitfalls: Using SOSL for exact filtering on known fields: SOQL is clearer and immediate.
Expecting just-inserted records in SOSL results within the same transaction.

quiz.q: You need every Account and Contact whose name contains 'acme'. Which fits best?
options: Two SOQL queries using LIKE '%acme%' on each object
One SOSL search returning Account and Contact
quiz.why: Searching text across several objects at once is what SOSL is for.

quiz.q: What does a SOSL query return in Apex?
quiz.why: One list per object named in RETURNING.

quiz.q: Which is true of SOSL compared with SOQL?
options: SOSL can filter on any field with exact matches, like SOQL
SOSL uses the search index, so very new records may not appear yet
quiz.why: SOSL reads the search index, which updates shortly after records change.

nodes.title: Collections and DML
nodes.summary: Lists, sets, maps, and saving records in bulk.
nodes.lesson:
Bulk-safe Apex is built on three collections:

- **List**: ordered, duplicates allowed. Queries return lists.
- **Set**: unique values, fast `contains`. Collect Ids into a `Set<Id>` before querying.
- **Map**: key to value. `new Map<Id, Account>([SELECT ...])` indexes records by Id in one line.

**DML** saves records: `insert`, `update`, `upsert` (by Id or an external Id), `delete`, `undelete`. Each statement can handle up to 10,000 records, so collect changes into a list and run **one** statement.

`Database.insert(records, false)` allows **partial success**: valid rows save, and each `SaveResult` says which failed and why. `Database.setSavepoint()` and `Database.rollback(sp)` undo work inside a transaction.
concepts: Choosing List, Set or Map
Building a Map<Id, SObject> straight from a query
One DML statement for a whole collection
Partial success with Database methods, and savepoints
pitfalls: DML inside a loop: 151 records and you've hit the 150-statement limit.
Using a List where uniqueness matters: duplicates sneak into your query filters.
Ignoring `SaveResult` errors after `Database.insert(list, false)`.

nodes.title: Errors and exceptions
nodes.summary: try/catch, custom exceptions, and showing errors to users.
nodes.lesson:
When something goes wrong, Apex **throws an exception**; unhandled, it rolls back the whole transaction.

- `try { … } catch (DmlException e) { … } finally { … }`: catch the specific types you can handle; `Exception` catches the rest.
- Custom exceptions: `public class BudgetException extends Exception {}`; the name must end in `Exception`.
- **`LimitException` can't be caught**: going over a governor limit always fails the transaction.
- In triggers, `record.addError('message')` stops that record's save and shows the message to the user, without failing the others in a partial-success save.
- Don't swallow errors: an empty `catch` hides the bug and leaves data half-changed.
concepts: try/catch/finally and catching specific exception types
Writing custom exceptions
Why LimitException can't be caught
addError for user-facing validation in triggers
pitfalls: An empty catch block that hides failures.
Catching Exception to 'handle' a limit problem: it can't be caught; fix the code.
Throwing in a trigger when `addError` would give the user a clean message.

quiz.q: Which exception can never be caught?
quiz.why: Exceeding a governor limit ends the transaction; catch blocks don't run.

quiz.q: Which is a valid custom exception?
quiz.why: Custom exceptions extend Exception and their name must end in Exception.

quiz.q: In a before trigger, how do you stop one bad record from saving with a friendly message?
options: throw new Exception('message') from the trigger
quiz.why: addError blocks that record and shows the message; other records in a partial save still succeed.

quiz.q: What happens to the transaction when an exception isn't caught?
options: Everything in the transaction rolls back
The data is saved but flagged
Only the last DML statement in the transaction is undone
quiz.why: An unhandled exception rolls back all DML in the transaction.

nodes.title: Testing
nodes.summary: Test classes, test data and assertions; 75% coverage to deploy.
nodes.lesson:
Every SFCode problem is graded by a hidden **test class**, the same way Salesforce gates production deploys.

- Mark classes `@IsTest`; methods `@IsTest static void ...`.
- Create your own data in the test. Never rely on org data (`SeeAllData=true`).
- Wrap the action in `Test.startTest()` / `Test.stopTest()`: you get fresh governor limits, and async work runs at `stopTest`.
- Assert outcomes with `Assert.areEqual(expected, actual, message)`.
- Production deploys need **75%** coverage overall and every trigger covered.

Test **bulk**: insert 200 records, not 1.

Also worth knowing:

- `@TestSetup` creates data once for every test method in the class.
- A **test data factory** class keeps record creation in one place.
- `System.runAs(user)` tests sharing and permissions as another user.
- `Test.setMock(HttpCalloutMock.class, mock)` fakes callouts; tests can't call real APIs.
concepts: @IsTest classes and methods; creating your own test data
Test.startTest/stopTest: fresh limits and running async work
Assertions that check behaviour, not just coverage
@TestSetup, data factories and System.runAs
pitfalls: Writing tests that only raise coverage and assert nothing.
Testing with one record: bulk bugs only show at 200.
Using SeeAllData=true: tests then break when org data changes.

quiz.q: What does Test.stopTest() do for asynchronous Apex queued in the test?
options: Schedules it to run after the test method finishes
Runs it before the next line
quiz.why: Async work queued between startTest and stopTest runs synchronously at stopTest.

quiz.q: What coverage does a production deploy require?
options: 100% of each class and trigger in the deployment
quiz.why: 75% overall across the Apex being deployed, and every trigger must have some coverage.

quiz.q: Why avoid SeeAllData=true?
options: It disables System.assert calls in the test
Tests then depend on org data and break when it changes
quiz.why: Tests should create their own data so they pass the same everywhere.

quiz.q: Which tests sharing as a specific user?
quiz.why: runAs executes the block as that user, applying their sharing.

nodes.title: Lightning Web Components
nodes.summary: Components, templates, reactivity and events.
nodes.lesson:
A **Lightning web component** is an HTML template, a JavaScript class and optional CSS.

- Fields on the class are **reactive**: reassign one and the template re-renders.
- `@api` makes a property public, so a parent can set it.
- Templates bind with `{property}` and can't hold expressions, so compute in **getters**: `get isEmpty() { return this.items.length === 0; }`.
- Lists use `for:each` with a unique `key`; conditions use `lwc:if` / `lwc:else`.
- Handlers are passed, not called: `onclick={handleClick}`.
concepts: Template, class and CSS; how they're wired
Reactivity, @api and getters
for:each with keys, lwc:if/lwc:else
Event handlers
pitfalls: Mutating an @api property inside the child: the parent owns it.
Writing an expression in a template (`{a + b}`): use a getter.
A for:each without a unique key.

nodes.title: Triggers
nodes.summary: Before/after context, bulk-safe patterns, recursion.
nodes.lesson:
A **trigger** is Apex that runs when records are inserted, updated, deleted or undeleted. It receives the records in **context variables**: `Trigger.new` (the new versions), `Trigger.old` (the previous ones, on update and delete), and the `Trigger.newMap` / `Trigger.oldMap` versions keyed by Id.

**Before** triggers run before the record is saved: change fields on `Trigger.new` directly and Salesforce saves them, with no DML. **After** triggers run once the record has an Id: use them to create or update *other* records.

Triggers fire for up to **200 records at a time**, so every trigger must be **bulk-safe**: no queries or DML inside loops. Collect what you need into sets and maps, query once, then loop.

Where triggers sit among everything else that happens on save is called the **order of execution**:
concepts: The difference between `Trigger.new`, `Trigger.old`, `Trigger.newMap` and `Trigger.oldMap`, and when each is null
Same-record field changes go in **before** triggers; changes to other records go in **after** triggers
Bulkification: one query and one DML statement per trigger run, whatever the batch size
One trigger per object, delegating to a handler class
How to stop recursion when an after trigger updates records that fire it again
pitfalls: Running `update` on `Trigger.new` in a before trigger: it fails. Assign the fields and let the save do it.
A SOQL query inside the loop: fine for one record in testing, a `LimitException` at 101 records.
Using `Trigger.old` in an insert trigger: it's null there.
Several triggers on one object: their order isn't guaranteed, so behaviour changes between deploys.

resources.title: Trigger and bulk request best practices

nodes.diagramCaption: Order of execution, simplified: before-save flows, before triggers, validation and duplicate rules, the save, after triggers, assignment rules, after-save flows, roll-ups, then commit and post-commit work.

quiz.q: Look at the diagram. A before-save flow and a before trigger both set the same field. Whose value is saved?
quiz.imageAlt: The order of execution: before-save flows run first, then before triggers, then validation rules.
quiz.why: Before-save flows run first (step 1) and before triggers run after them (step 2), so the trigger's assignment is the one that's saved.

quiz.q: Using the diagram: a validation rule fails. Has the after trigger run?
quiz.imageAlt: The order of execution: validation rules are step 3, after triggers are step 6.
options: Only if the trigger is active
No: validation fails before the save, and after triggers come after it
Yes, after triggers always run, even when validation fails
quiz.why: Validation runs before the record is saved (step 3). A failure stops the save, so steps 5 onwards, including after triggers, never run.

quiz.q: Where should you set a field on the same record that's being inserted?
options: Before insert trigger, assigning on Trigger.new
After insert trigger with an update statement
quiz.why: Before triggers can change Trigger.new directly; the save writes the change with no extra DML.

quiz.q: Which context variable is null in an insert trigger?
quiz.why: There's no previous version of a record being inserted, so Trigger.old and Trigger.oldMap are null.

nodes.title: Secure Apex
nodes.summary: Sharing, CRUD and FLS in code, and SOQL injection.
nodes.lesson:
Apex runs in **system mode**, so security is something your code opts into:

- **Record sharing**: declare `with sharing` on classes that serve users; `without sharing` only where you deliberately need to see everything; `inherited sharing` to follow the caller.
- **Object and field permissions**: query `WITH USER_MODE` (enforces CRUD, FLS and sharing), or run DML as the user with `insert as user records;`. `Security.stripInaccessible()` removes fields the user can't see from records.
- **SOQL injection**: never build queries by joining user input into a string. Use **bind variables** (`WHERE Name = :input`), which work in dynamic SOQL too, or `String.escapeSingleQuotes` as a last resort.
- Expose only what's needed from `@AuraEnabled` methods: they're callable by any user who can load the component.
concepts: with sharing, without sharing and inherited sharing
WITH USER_MODE and DML as user
Security.stripInaccessible
Bind variables against SOQL injection
pitfalls: Leaving a class without a sharing keyword: it runs without sharing when called from some contexts.
Building dynamic SOQL with string concatenation of user input.
Trusting the UI to hide data: an @AuraEnabled method returns whatever it queries.

quiz.q: Which clause enforces object permissions, field-level security and sharing in a query?
quiz.why: USER_MODE applies the running user's CRUD, FLS and sharing.

quiz.q: What stops SOQL injection?
options: Bind variables (:value) instead of joining strings
Running the query in system mode
quiz.why: Binds send input as a value, so it can't change the query's structure.

quiz.q: A class has no sharing keyword. Is sharing enforced?
options: Always, because sharing is on by default
It depends on the calling context; declare it explicitly
quiz.why: Without a keyword the class takes its sharing from context, which is easy to get wrong. Be explicit.

nodes.title: Debugging
nodes.summary: Debug logs, checkpoints and reading a stack trace.
nodes.lesson:
- **Debug logs** record what a transaction did. Set a **trace flag** for a user, reproduce the problem, then read the log: `USER_DEBUG` lines show your `System.debug` output; `SOQL_EXECUTE` and `DML_BEGIN` show queries and saves; `LIMIT_USAGE` shows how close you came to each limit.
- Log levels per category (Apex code, database, workflow…) control how much detail you get; too much detail truncates long logs.
- A **stack trace** names the class, method and line: start at the top line that's your code.
- The SFCode **Apex Playground** shows debug output and limit usage for anonymous Apex in your connected org.
concepts: Trace flags and log levels
Reading USER_DEBUG, SOQL_EXECUTE and limit usage
Finding your code in a stack trace
pitfalls: Leaving very verbose log levels on: logs truncate and hide the part you need.
Leaving `System.debug` of sensitive data in production code.

quiz.q: Which debug log event shows your System.debug output?
quiz.why: System.debug writes USER_DEBUG lines.

quiz.q: What must exist before a user's actions produce debug logs?
options: A permission set with View All Data for that user
A trace flag for that user
quiz.why: Trace flags turn logging on for a user, class or trigger for a period of time.

quiz.q: Why turn log levels down rather than up when a log is huge?
options: Lower levels download faster, but show the same detail
Logs have a size cap; too much detail truncates the part you need
quiz.why: Logs over the size limit are truncated, often losing the end where the error is.

nodes.title: LWC and data
nodes.summary: Wire service, Lightning Data Service and calling Apex.
nodes.lesson:
- **Lightning Data Service** (`getRecord`, `updateRecord`, `lightning-record-form`) reads and writes single records with sharing and FLS applied, and keeps a shared cache, so every component showing a record updates together.
- **`@wire`** connects a property or function to a data source and re-runs when its reactive parameters (`$recordId`) change.
- **Apex**: annotate methods `@AuraEnabled(cacheable=true)` to use them with `@wire`; call non-cacheable ones imperatively for DML. After changing data, `refreshApex(wiredResult)` refreshes a wired Apex result.
- State that drives lists should be replaced, not mutated: `this.items = [...this.items, item]`.
concepts: Lightning Data Service and its shared cache
@wire with reactive `$` parameters
cacheable=true versus imperative Apex calls
refreshApex after a change
pitfalls: DML in a `cacheable=true` method: it fails.
Forgetting refreshApex, so the list stays stale after an update.
Querying a single record with Apex when Lightning Data Service would do it with security built in.

resources.title: Lightning Web Components and Salesforce Data (Trailhead)

nodes.title: Trigger architecture
nodes.summary: One trigger per object, handler classes, recursion control.
nodes.lesson:
As an org grows, triggers need structure:

- **One trigger per object**, with no logic in it: it hands every event to a **handler class**. Several triggers on one object run in an undefined order.
- The handler routes by event (`beforeInsert`, `afterUpdate`…) to methods or **service** classes that hold the business logic, with **selector** classes holding the queries.
- **Recursion**: an after trigger that updates related records can fire triggers again. A static `Set<Id>` of already-processed records stops repeat work within one transaction.
- Keep switches to turn handlers off (custom metadata), for data loads and emergencies.
concepts: One trigger per object, logic in a handler
Service and selector classes
Static recursion guards
Bypass switches with custom metadata
pitfalls: A static Boolean 'run once' flag: it skips the second chunk of 200 in a bulk load. Track Ids instead.
Logic split across several triggers on the same object.
nodes.diagramCaption: Trigger handler pattern: a one-line trigger calls a handler, which routes to service and selector classes and uses a static recursion guard.

quiz.q: Look at the diagram. Where does the business logic live?
options: In AccountTrigger itself, in each context block
In the handler and the service and selector classes it calls
quiz.why: The trigger is one line; the handler routes to classes that hold the logic and queries.
quiz.imageAlt: Diagram: AccountTrigger calls AccountTriggerHandler, which calls AccountService and AccountSelector, with a recursion guard.

quiz.q: Using the diagram, what does the recursion guard store?
options: A Boolean flag set once the trigger has run
A static Set<Id> of records already processed
quiz.why: Tracking Ids handles bulk loads correctly, where a single flag would skip later chunks.
quiz.imageAlt: Diagram: the recursion guard box reads 'static Set<Id> already processed'.

quiz.q: Why only one trigger per object?
options: Salesforce allows only one trigger per object, so a second won't save
Multiple triggers on one object run in no guaranteed order
quiz.why: With several triggers, execution order isn't defined, so behaviour can change between deploys.

nodes.title: Governor limits
nodes.summary: The limits every transaction lives within, and how to stay under them.
nodes.lesson:
Every transaction has hard limits. The ones you'll meet most (synchronous / asynchronous):

| Limit | Sync | Async |
|---|---|---|
| SOQL queries | 100 | 200 |
| Records returned by SOQL | 50,000 | 50,000 |
| DML statements | 150 | 150 |
| Records processed by DML | 10,000 | 10,000 |
| CPU time | 10 s | 60 s |
| Heap | 6 MB | 12 MB |
| Callouts | 100 | 100 |

Staying under them is a design habit: query once outside loops, DML once on collections, filter in SOQL rather than in Apex, and move large volumes to Batch Apex. `Limits.getQueries()` and friends tell you where you are.
concepts: The main limits and their sync/async values
Bulk patterns that keep you under them
Measuring with the Limits class
When to move work to async or Batch
pitfalls: Trying to catch a LimitException: you can't.
Filtering records in Apex loops when SOQL could have filtered them.
Loading huge lists into memory and hitting the heap limit.

nodes.title: Callouts and integration
nodes.summary: HTTP callouts, JSON, Named Credentials and mocks.
nodes.lesson:
Apex calls other systems with `HttpRequest` and `Http.send()`:

- Store the endpoint and authentication in a **Named Credential** and call `callout:My_API/path`: no secrets in code, and no Remote Site Setting needed.
- Parse JSON with typed classes (`JSON.deserialize(body, MyResponse.class)`) or `JSON.deserializeUntyped`.
- Check the status code before trusting the body; set timeouts.
- **Callouts can't run after uncommitted DML** in the same transaction, and triggers can't call out directly: use Queueable (with `Database.AllowsCallouts`) or `@future(callout=true)`.
- In tests, `Test.setMock(HttpCalloutMock.class, mock)` returns a fake response.
concepts: HttpRequest, Http.send and status codes
Named Credentials instead of hard-coded URLs and secrets
JSON serialisation and parsing
Callouts from triggers via async Apex
HttpCalloutMock in tests
pitfalls: Hard-coding API keys in Apex or custom settings.
Calling out after DML in the same transaction: 'You have uncommitted work pending'.
Parsing the body without checking the status code.
nodes.diagramCaption: Callouts: Apex sends an HttpRequest to a Named Credential, which holds the URL and authentication and calls the external API; tests use HttpCalloutMock.

quiz.q: Look at the diagram. Where should the API's URL and credentials live?
options: In a custom label per environment
quiz.why: Named Credentials hold the endpoint and auth so code never contains secrets.
quiz.imageAlt: Diagram: Apex calls a Named Credential, which holds URL and auth and calls the external API.

quiz.q: Using the diagram's notes: what answers callouts during a test?
options: The real API, called from the test with a test key
quiz.why: Tests can't make real callouts; a mock returns the response.
quiz.imageAlt: Diagram notes: in tests, Test.setMock with an HttpCalloutMock answers instead of the API.

quiz.q: A trigger must call an external API. What do you do?
options: Enqueue a Queueable (or @future(callout=true)) that makes the callout
Call Http.send directly in the trigger after the save
quiz.why: Triggers can't make callouts synchronously; async Apex can.

nodes.title: LWC communication
nodes.summary: Events up, properties down, and Lightning Message Service.
nodes.lesson:
- **Parent to child**: set the child's `@api` properties, or call its `@api` methods.
- **Child to parent**: `this.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('select', { detail: id }))`; the parent listens with `onselect={handleSelect}`. Event names are lower-case.
- `bubbles` and `composed` let events travel further up or out of shadow DOM; use them sparingly.
- **Unrelated components** (different parts of a page, or LWC talking to Aura and Visualforce) use **Lightning Message Service**: publish to and subscribe on a **message channel**.
concepts: @api properties and methods
CustomEvent with detail; lower-case event names
bubbles and composed
Lightning Message Service channels
pitfalls: Using camelCase event names: listeners won't match.
Reaching into a child's DOM to change it instead of using @api.
Reaching for LMS between a parent and its child, where events and properties are simpler.
nodes.diagramCaption: LWC communication: a parent passes data down with @api properties, a child sends CustomEvents up, and unrelated components publish and subscribe through a Lightning Message Service channel.

quiz.q: Look at the diagram. A child must tell its parent a star was clicked. How?
options: Dispatch a CustomEvent the parent listens for
Set a property on the parent
Publish to a Lightning message channel
quiz.why: Children send changes up as events; properties only flow down.
quiz.imageAlt: Diagram: arrows show @api props down from c-parent to c-child and CustomEvent up from child to parent.

quiz.q: Using the diagram, how do c-child and c-unrelated communicate?
options: Through the parent's template, passing values down with @api
Through a Lightning Message Service channel: one publishes, the other subscribes
quiz.why: Components with no parent-child link use a message channel.
quiz.imageAlt: Diagram: c-child publishes to a Message channel; c-unrelated subscribes to it.

quiz.q: Which event name will a parent's `onitemselect` handler receive?
quiz.why: Event names are lower-case, and `on` plus the name forms the handler attribute.

nodes.title: Asynchronous Apex
nodes.summary: Future, Queueable and choosing the right async tool.
nodes.lesson:
Async Apex runs later, in its own transaction, with **higher limits** (200 queries, 12 MB heap, 60 s CPU):

- **@future**: a static method with primitive arguments. Simple, but can't be chained or monitored easily.
- **Queueable**: a class with `execute(QueueableContext)`; takes objects as arguments, returns a job Id from `System.enqueueJob`, and can **chain** another job. The default choice today.
- **Batch Apex** and **Schedulable** handle volume and timing; see the next step.
- **Platform Events** decouple work: publish an event, and subscribers handle it.

Async work doesn't start until the transaction that queued it **commits**.
concepts: @future versus Queueable
Higher async limits
Chaining Queueable jobs
Async starts only after commit
pitfalls: Calling @future from @future or from Batch: not allowed.
Enqueuing a Queueable per record inside a loop.
Expecting async results within the same transaction.
nodes.diagramCaption: Choosing asynchronous Apex: future for simple deferred work, Queueable for objects and chaining, Batch for millions of records, Schedulable for timed runs, Platform Events to notify other systems.

quiz.q: Look at the diagram. You need to pass a List<Account> to code that runs later and then start a second job. Which tool?
quiz.why: Queueable takes objects as arguments and can chain jobs.
quiz.imageAlt: Diagram: Queueable is labelled 'Run later, objects as args, chain jobs'.

quiz.q: Using the diagram, which tool processes millions of records in chunks?
quiz.why: Batch Apex splits a large dataset into chunks, each with its own limits.
quiz.imageAlt: Diagram: Batch Apex is labelled 'Millions of records in chunks'.

quiz.q: How many SOQL queries may an asynchronous transaction run?
quiz.why: Async limits are higher: 200 queries instead of 100.

nodes.title: Batch and scheduled Apex
nodes.summary: Processing large volumes in chunks, on a schedule.
nodes.lesson:
**Batch Apex** processes up to 50 million records:

- `start` returns a `Database.QueryLocator` (or an iterable) describing the records.
- `execute` receives a **chunk** (200 by default, set in `Database.executeBatch(job, size)`), each with fresh limits.
- `finish` runs once at the end: send a summary, chain another job.
- `Database.Stateful` keeps instance variables between chunks; without it they reset.

**Schedulable** classes run at set times: `System.schedule('Nightly', '0 0 2 * * ?', new MyJob())`. A common pattern is a scheduled class that starts a batch.
concepts: start, execute and finish
Chunk size and per-chunk limits
Database.Stateful
Cron expressions with System.schedule
pitfalls: Querying the same records again inside execute: the scope already has them.
Expecting counters to survive between chunks without Database.Stateful.
Too many scheduled jobs: orgs have a cap on scheduled Apex.

nodes.title: Platform events
nodes.summary: Publish-subscribe messaging inside and outside Salesforce.
nodes.lesson:
A **platform event** is a message type you define (`Order_Shipped__e`) with fields. Code, Flows and external systems **publish** events; triggers, Flows, LWC and external subscribers **receive** them.

- Publish from Apex with `EventBus.publish(events)`; check the `SaveResult`s.
- By default events are delivered **after the transaction commits** (Publish After Commit), so subscribers never see work that was rolled back.
- Event triggers run as the Automated Process user in their own transaction, and can process events in batches.
- They decouple systems: the publisher doesn't need to know who's listening.
concepts: Defining an event and its fields
Publishing with EventBus.publish
Publish After Commit versus Publish Immediately
Subscribers: triggers, flows, LWC, external
pitfalls: Using platform events for data that must be queryable later: they're messages, not records.
Expecting the subscriber to run as the user who published.

quiz.q: How do you publish a platform event from Apex?
quiz.why: EventBus.publish sends the event and returns SaveResults.

quiz.q: With 'Publish After Commit', what happens if the publishing transaction rolls back?
quiz.why: After-commit events are only sent when the transaction succeeds.

quiz.q: Which can subscribe to a platform event?
options: Only Apex triggers on the event object
Triggers, Flows, LWC and external systems
quiz.why: Platform events support many subscriber types, which is what makes them good for decoupling.

nodes.title: Performance at scale
nodes.summary: Selective queries, indexes and large data volumes.
nodes.lesson:
With millions of records, the question becomes whether your query is **selective**: does it filter on an **indexed** field (Id, Name, lookups, external Ids, and fields you ask Salesforce to index) narrowly enough to avoid scanning the whole table?

- Non-selective queries in triggers fail outright on large objects.
- Avoid leading wildcards (`LIKE '%acme'`), `!=` and `NOT IN` on big tables: they can't use indexes well.
- **Data skew**: one parent with tens of thousands of children (or one owner of huge numbers of records) causes lock contention and slow sharing recalculation.
- Use **Batch Apex** and the **Bulk API** for big loads; turn off non-essential automation during data migrations.
concepts: Selective queries and standard indexes
Why leading wildcards and negative filters are slow
Ownership and parent-child data skew
Batch and Bulk API for large volumes
pitfalls: A trigger query filtering on an unindexed field: fine in a sandbox, fails in production at volume.
Assigning millions of records to a single integration user.

quiz.q: Which filter is most likely to be selective?
options: WHERE Description != null AND Name != null
quiz.why: External ID fields are indexed; an equality filter on one is selective.

quiz.q: What is data skew?
options: Records with bad or missing data in key fields
One parent or owner with a huge number of child or owned records
quiz.why: Skew causes locking and slow sharing calculations.

quiz.q: You must load 5 million records. What's appropriate?
options: Data Import Wizard in batches of 50,000 records
Bulk API or Data Loader in bulk mode, with heavy automation paused
quiz.why: Bulk API is built for large volumes; pausing non-essential automation avoids limits and locks.

nodes.title: Deployment and DevOps
nodes.summary: Getting changes safely from development to production.
nodes.lesson:
Changes move through environments: build in a scratch org or sandbox, commit to **Git**, test automatically in **CI**, check in a UAT sandbox, then deploy to production.

- **Salesforce CLI** deploys source: `sf project deploy start --test-level RunLocalTests`.
- Production deploys **run tests**: overall coverage of at least 75%, every trigger covered, all tests passing.
- Alternatives: **change sets** (clicks, between connected orgs), **unlocked packages** (versioned modules), **DevOps Center**.
- Validate first (`--dry-run`) and quick-deploy the validated build in your release window.
- Data isn't deployed with metadata: plan data loads separately.
concepts: Environments: scratch org, sandbox, UAT, production
Deploying with the Salesforce CLI and test levels
Coverage rules for production
Change sets, packages and DevOps Center
pitfalls: Deploying on release night without a prior validation.
Assuming records come with a metadata deploy.
Different metadata in sandboxes than in Git: everything should come from source.
nodes.diagramCaption: Deployment pipeline: build in a scratch org or sandbox, commit to Git, run tests in CI, check in a UAT sandbox, then deploy to production.

quiz.q: Look at the diagram. Where should automated tests run before anything reaches production?
options: Only in the scratch org of the developer who made the change
In CI, after the change is committed to Git
quiz.why: CI runs the tests on every change, before UAT and production.
quiz.imageAlt: Diagram: Scratch org, Git, CI (tests, scans), UAT sandbox, Production.

quiz.q: Using the diagram's note: what must be true for a production deploy?
options: 75% overall coverage, every trigger covered, all tests pass
No tests are needed when deploying with change sets
quiz.why: Production deploys enforce those test rules.
quiz.imageAlt: Diagram note: production deploys need 75% org-wide coverage, every trigger covered, all tests passing.

quiz.q: Which is versioned and installable as a module?
options: A change set, which can be reinstalled
quiz.why: Packages are versioned units of metadata.

nodes.title: Design patterns
nodes.summary: Service, domain and selector layers for larger codebases.
nodes.lesson:
**Apex Enterprise Patterns** organise big codebases into layers:

- **Selector**: all the queries for an object, in one place, with consistent fields and security.
- **Domain**: behaviour and validation for an object's records (what a trigger handler calls).
- **Service**: business operations that span objects (`OpportunityService.applyDiscount(ids, pct)`), callable from LWC, REST, batch or triggers alike.
- **Unit of Work**: collect DML and commit it once, in the right order.

Not every org needs all four: the goal is code where each class has one reason to change.
concepts: Selector, domain, service and unit of work layers
Separation of concerns
When patterns help and when they're overkill
pitfalls: Adopting a full framework for three triggers.
Putting queries everywhere instead of in selectors: fields and security drift.

resources.title: Apex Enterprise Patterns: Domain and Selector Layers (Trailhead)

quiz.q: Which layer holds an object's queries?
quiz.why: Selectors centralise SOQL for an object.

quiz.q: Which layer exposes business operations to LWC, REST and batch alike?
quiz.why: Service methods are the single entry point for an operation, whoever calls it.

quiz.q: What does a Unit of Work do?
options: Schedules jobs in the order they were queued
Collects DML and commits it once, in order
quiz.why: It batches DML across objects into one ordered commit.

nodes.summary: Exposing your own REST endpoints from Salesforce.
concepts: @RestResource and the HTTP method annotations
RestContext request and response
Authentication via Connected Apps and integration users
When to use the standard REST API instead
